events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Amara proposes Amara, Maya. As a Loyal Servant, I know my own allegiance is Good, so including myself ensures at least one reliable Good member. I am pairing with Maya to test the waters and open discussion.

Amara’s proposal is only two people, so any single Evil member would be enough to fail Mission 1. Amara’s self-inclusion rests on her claim to be a Loyal Servant; from my seat that is a public claim, not verification. Maya is the other proposed member, and I have not heard her rationale yet. I am not rejecting the team reflexively, but I do not want to approve solely because the leader vouches for herself. Maya, do you support Amara’s reasoning and would you vote yes on this exact pair, or do you think the team should be revised before the vote?

Zara raised a fair question about whether I support Amara's reasoning and would vote yes on this exact pair, so I will answer it directly. Yes, I support the team of Amara and myself, and I would vote yes as it stands. On Amara's self-vouching: I agree with Zara that a leader claiming Loyal Servant is a claim, not proof. I will not lean on that claim either, since I cannot verify anyone's role. But my support does not rest on Amara's claim. It rests on the structure of this mission. With five players, Mission 1 takes a team of two, and any two-player team carries the same structural risk Zara identified: one Evil member fails it. There is no possible first proposal that avoids that risk, so the real question is which pair gives us the most information if it fails and the cleanest signal if it succeeds. A small first team does exactly that. If it succeeds, we learn this pair is likely clear, or at least that Evil declined to spend a Fail here, which is itself informative. If it fails, the suspicion radius is only two people instead of three or four, and the rest of us get sharper reads on the remaining proposals. Waiting for a larger or 'safer' team does not actually reduce the risk on Mission 1; it just blurs the information we get back. On my own position: I am happy to be on this team and to be tested by the result. If this mission fails, I should be treated as a primary suspect alongside Amara, and I accept that burden openly. I would rather be inside a testable pair than standing outside it making claims I cannot prove. So my answer to Zara's exact question is yes on this exact pair, before any revision, and I am not asking Amara to change it. I want a decision here rather than a rotation through proposals that all carry the same single-Evil risk.

Maya, your answer is direct, and your point about Mission 1’s unavoidable two-person risk is fair. But accepting that risk does not make this specific pair the right one. Amara proposed herself and you, and her stated reason was that she knows her own allegiance and wants to test the waters. That is not independent evidence about your allegiance, and it does not explain why Isha or Noah were left out. A first team should give us more than a narrow suspicion radius; it should also test the leader’s judgment. I am not convinced that all two-person teams are equivalent here. If this team succeeds, we may learn little because Evil could simply decline to fail; if it fails, we still have to weigh Amara and you against the possibility that the proposal was designed to be approved. I would rather hear a stronger case from Amara or see a revision before I support this exact pair. At present I am inclined to reject it.

I would approve Amara and Maya. We have no mission results yet, and Amara including herself is a reasonable starting point, even though her claim is not proof. Zara is right that a success would not clear the pair definitively, but a failure would still give us a useful, narrow starting point. I don't see enough reason to revise this team before the first vote.

I remain opposed to the exact team of Amara and Maya. Amara’s rationale is self-referential: she says she knows her own allegiance, but that is a claim from her seat, not evidence available to the rest of us. The proposal also does not explain why Isha or Noah were excluded, and Maya’s support for the pair does not supply independent verification of either proposed member. Maya is right that any two-person Mission 1 team carries single-Evil risk, but that does not make all such teams equally sound. A leader’s first proposal should test judgment as well as loyalty, and this one gives me little reason to approve it before a revision. I would rather see Amara revise the team or give a stronger case. At present I am inclined to reject this exact pair.

Zara, I understand your scrutiny, but on Mission 1 with zero track record or voting history, any rationale for picking a partner is necessarily exploratory. A leader proposing themselves is standard practice because from my own perspective, it leaves only one unknown slot instead of two. Maya and Isha have both shared their perspectives, but Noah has not yet spoken on this proposal. Noah, what is your stance on approving this team of Maya and myself, and do you see a clear reason to revise it before we head to a vote?

Amara, to answer your question directly: I support approving the team of Amara and Maya, and I see no clear reason to revise it before the vote. Zara is right that Amara's self-inclusion is a claim, not proof, and we should treat it that way. But on Mission 1 every two-person team carries the same single-Fail risk, and Maya has answered Zara's question on this exact pair. A first team that is small and testable gives us the most information if it fails, and a clean signal if it succeeds. Waiting for a different pair does not reduce that risk. I would rather we reach a decision and learn from the result than keep rotating proposals. I will approve this team.

My position is unchanged: I support approving Amara and Maya. Zara is right that Amara's self-inclusion is a claim, not verification, and we should weigh it that way. But no one at this table can verify any role yet, so the vote should turn on the team's risk and what it tells us. Every two-person Mission 1 team carries the same single-Fail risk, and Maya has answered the direct question about this pair. If we keep rejecting proposals, we spend rejections without learning anything about the leader or the team. I'd rather approve this pair, see the mission result, and then judge the next proposal on what we learn.

This is my final word on the proposal. I approve Amara and Maya. Amara's self-inclusion is a claim, not proof, and we should weigh it that way. Maya has answered the direct question about this exact pair, and every two-person Mission 1 team carries the same single-Fail risk. Rejecting this team would spend a rejection without giving us information. If the mission fails, we will have a narrow suspicion radius to work from, and I will judge the next proposal on what that result shows.

Zara, I want to address your latest objection directly, because I think it rests on a standard no first proposal could actually meet. You say a first team should test the leader's judgment as well as loyalty, and that Amara has not explained why Isha or Noah were left out. But on Mission 1 with a team size of two, any leader must leave out two of four other players, and there is no rationale for any exclusion that would constitute evidence rather than preference. If Amara had chosen Isha, you could ask the same question about Noah and me. This critique applies to every possible pair at this table, which means it cannot be the reason to prefer one pair over another. What we actually know so far: I support this pair and would vote yes, Isha approves it, Noah has approved it three times and given his final word, and Amara has answered your challenge as fully as anyone can with zero results on the board. That is four players willing to move forward and one holding out for a stronger case that the game structure cannot yet provide. You also argue that a success teaches us little because Evil might decline to fail, and that a failure still leaves you weighing the pair against the possibility that the proposal was designed to be approved. Both points are true, but neither is an argument against this pair specifically — they are arguments against playing Mission 1 at all. Every team carries those exact properties. Meanwhile, rejecting this proposal has a concrete cost: it spends one of five rejections, burns Amara's leadership, and gives us no new information, because we would simply rotate to another two-person team with the same single-Evil risk you already acknowledged. I accept the burden I stated earlier: if this mission fails, I am a primary suspect alongside Amara, and I will not hide from that. That is a real, testable commitment, unlike waiting for evidence that cannot exist before the first mission resolves. I am voting yes on this exact pair, and I would rather we learn from the result than spend rejections avoiding a risk no team can escape.
Amara confirms Amara, Maya. A clear majority of the table—Maya, Isha, Noah, and myself—supports testing this pair on Mission 1. I am keeping the team as Amara and Maya.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Maya proposes Maya, Amara, Isha. As leader, I am keeping the proven Mission 1 pair together: Amara and I both passed the test and accepted accountability, and Mission 1 succeeded with zero fails. Adding Isha expands the team by one, so if this mission fails, the suspicion radius includes exactly one new player alongside a vetted pair, giving us the sharpest possible information from the result. Isha was also an early, clear supporter of moving forward, though I weight that lightly since votes alone prove nothing. Zara's rejection of the last team was dissent, not evidence of Evil, and Noah made a solid case, but with three slots I can only add one new name to a known-good core, and Isha is my choice. If this mission succeeds, both Isha and this pair gain credibility; if it fails, we learn a great deal about exactly who among the three is suspect.

Maya, I do not accept that Amara and you are a "proven" pair. Mission 1 succeeding with zero fails is consistent with both of you being Good, but it is also consistent with Evil choosing not to fail a two-person team. That result does not verify either of you, and it cannot carry the weight you place on it now. The new element is Isha. Your stated reason for adding her is that she was an early, clear supporter of moving forward, but votes and support are not evidence of allegiance; they are exactly what Evil can offer freely. If the strongest case for Isha is that she approved the previous team, then this proposal is adding an unverified third player to an unverified core and calling the combination sharp. I would rather see a rationale that distinguishes Isha from Noah or me, or a revision that explains why this exact three is the best test. Noah, you argued last round for approving the Amara-Maya pair and said you would judge the next proposal on what the result showed. What independent reason, beyond Isha's prior vote, supports putting her on this team now—and if there is none, would you still approve this exact three? At present I am inclined to reject.

Zara, to answer your question directly: my reason is not Isha's earlier vote alone. Mission 1 succeeded with the Amara and Maya pair, and Maya has kept that core and added one new name, which keeps the team at three and limits how much a single failure could implicate. Isha has stated her position clearly, and I have no evidence against her. I agree that votes are not proof of allegiance, so I am not treating her approval as verification. I would approve this exact three because the mission needs three players, every alternative would again add unverified names, and rejecting now would spend a rejection on the same single-Fail risk we already accepted. If this mission fails, we will have a narrow group to examine, and I will judge the next proposal on that result. I approve Maya, Amara, and Isha.

I remain opposed to this exact team. Maya’s case still treats the Mission 1 result as if it verified Amara and her, but a zero-fail success on a two-person team is not proof; Evil can simply choose not to fail. That matters because the proposed core is being given credit it has not earned. The only new element is Isha, and the rationale for adding her is still her earlier support for moving forward. That is not independent evidence of allegiance; it is exactly the kind of public behavior any Evil player can mimic. Noah’s answer confirms this rather than resolving it: he says he has no evidence against Isha and would approve because the mission needs three players and rejecting spends a rejection. Absence of evidence is not a reason to put someone on a team, and “we must decide” is not a rationale that distinguishes Isha from anyone else. All three proposed members remain unverified, and the leader has not explained why this exact three is a better test than a revision. I would reject this exact team and ask the next leader to provide a sharper case or a different composition. At present I am firmly inclined to vote no.

Maya, I still reject the premise that Mission 1 verified Amara and you. A zero-fail two-person result is compatible with Evil declining to fail, so the core has not earned the trust you are giving it. That matters because the only new player is Isha, and the stated reason for her is that she supported moving forward. Public support is exactly what any Evil player can offer without cost; it is not independent evidence. Noah's answer did not supply one either, but at least he has not been on a mission and has stated a clear decision rule. If you are determined to keep Amara and yourself, the third slot should test a genuinely untested player rather than reward prior approval. Will you revise the team to Maya, Amara, Noah? If you keep Isha, I will vote no on this exact three, because the rationale still does not distinguish her from Noah or me.

Zara, I will answer your revision request directly rather than sidestep it. You ask me to swap Isha for Noah and call that a sharper test. But your own argument dismantles that request. You have said, correctly, that votes and public support are not evidence of allegiance, that absence of evidence against someone is not a reason to trust them, and that no rationale for exclusion on Mission 1 constitutes evidence rather than preference. Apply that standard to your proposed revision: what evidence distinguishes Noah from Isha? None. Noah has not been on a mission, but neither has Isha. Noah stated a clear decision rule, but so has Isha. By the very criteria you have laid out, Isha and Noah are equally unverified, which means your request to swap them is not a demand for a sharper test — it is a demand that I reward the player who happened to dissent from the last team. You explicitly conceded that Zara's rejection was dissent, not evidence of Evil, when Amara said it in the last round; the same logic cuts both ways. Isha supported moving forward, you opposed it, and neither behavior tells us anything about allegiance. So I will not trade one unverified player for another and call it responsiveness. My reasoning for this three stands: Amara and I accepted accountability on Mission 1 and delivered a clean result, and Isha is the one new name, so a failure would focus suspicion on exactly one additional person alongside a tested pair. That is the sharpest information structure available, and no revision you have proposed improves it. I am keeping Maya, Amara, and Isha, and I will vote yes on this exact team. Zara, you have now had two full turns laying out why you would reject. I have a direct question before we go to a vote: if I accepted your revision to Maya, Amara, and Noah, what specific reason beyond Noah's prior opposition would make that three a better test than this one — and if the answer is none, as your own stated standard implies, will you vote yes on this exact team?

I support Maya's proposal of Maya, Amara, and Isha. Speaking from my own perspective, I know I am Good, so keeping myself on the team ensures at least one slot is genuinely Loyal. The Maya-Amara pair delivered a clean result on Mission 1, and expanding by exactly one player is the most controlled way to test a three-person mission. Zara has spent three turns aggressively lobbying to swap Isha for Noah, but as Maya rightly pointed out, there is zero objective track record that makes Noah inherently safer than Isha. Zara's stance feels like arbitrary obstruction rather than constructive vetting. Isha, you have been selected for this third slot and have not spoken yet this round: what is your stance on this team, and how do you respond to Zara's push to replace you?

Amara, I support this team and will vote yes. I know my own allegiance, so from my perspective adding me to the pair that succeeded on Mission 1 is a reasonable way to build on that result. The success does not prove Maya or Amara are Good, and I understand why Zara wants that distinction made. But replacing me with Noah would not make the earlier result any more conclusive, and I see no public evidence that makes him a better choice. I would keep Maya, Amara, and Isha.

I approve Maya, Amara, and Isha. Mission 1 succeeded with the Amara and Maya core, and keeping that core while adding one new name limits how much a single failure could implicate. Isha has stated her position clearly, and I have no evidence against her. Swapping her for Noah would only trade one unverified player for another, and I would rather test this team than spend another rejection. I will vote yes on this exact team.

I am keeping my position on Maya, Amara, and Isha. Mission 1 succeeded with the Amara and Maya core, and Maya has added one new name, so a failure would still narrow the group to three players. Isha has answered the revision question directly and clearly, and no one has offered public evidence that Noah is a safer choice than Isha. The discussion has covered the same ground several times, so I think we should move to the vote and judge the result of Mission 2 on what it shows.

Maya confirms Maya, Amara, Isha. I am keeping Maya, Amara, and Isha. The core pair delivered a clean Mission 1 result and accepted accountability, Isha is the single new addition so a failure would focus suspicion narrowly, and the table—Noah, Isha, Amara—has answered every challenge including Zara's swap request, which by Zara's own standard offers no evidence distinguishing Noah from Isha. Moving to a vote.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Noah proposes Noah, Isha. Mission 2 succeeded with the Maya, Amara, and Isha team, so Mission 3 needs two players. I am proposing myself with Isha: Isha has backed the proposals that succeeded so far, and two members with no record yet gives a clean, testable read if this mission fails.

I will vote no on Noah and Isha. I know my own allegiance, but Noah has not been on a successful mission, and his rationale incorrectly describes both of us as having no record: I was on the successful Mission 2 team. He also voted against that team after repeatedly saying he would approve it, which makes me cautious about his stated reasoning now.

I would rather return to Maya and Amara, the pair that succeeded on Mission 1. That success does not prove either is Good, but replacing one of them with Noah introduces an untested player when we are one success away from the assassination phase.

Noah, your proposal has a factual problem: Isha is not without a record. She was on the successful Mission 2 team, and you voted against that team after saying you would approve it. Isha is right to flag that inconsistency. I have been the table’s skeptic about treating success as proof, and I still do. But this is Mission 3, the team size is two, and we are one success from the assassination phase. Rejecting every unverified pair is not a strategy; it spends rejections and hands leadership around without producing a fail card. The proposed team at least contains Isha, whose mission record I can weigh, and if it is approved she can personally ensure her card is Success while we finally test Noah. Isha, you said you would vote no. If you vote no and this team is rejected, leadership likely passes to you and we still have no new mission result; if you vote yes, you are on the team and can control your own card. Would you reconsider and vote yes on this exact pair to test Noah under your own observation?

Zara, I will not reconsider. Being on the team lets me control my own card, but it does not let me observe or control Noah’s card. A failure would cost us a chance to end the missions now.

Noah’s vote against Mission 2 after repeatedly promising to approve it, together with his mistaken description of my record, gives me reason to prefer the Maya-Amara pair that already succeeded. That success is not proof, but we have no rejected teams on this mission and can afford to seek a stronger proposal.

Noah, will you revise the team to Maya and Amara, and can you explain why you voted against Mission 2 after saying you would approve it?

Isha, you are right on one point and I was wrong on another. Mission 2 succeeded with you on the team, so my claim that you had no record was a factual error, and I should not have made it. I also voted against Mission 2 after saying I would approve it. I was still weighing Zara's concern about adding an untested name and did not restate that before voting, so the vote looked inconsistent. That was a communication failure on my part, and I own it.

On your request: I will not revise to Maya and Amara. That pair has already been tested together on Mission 1, and both were on the successful Mission 2 team. Putting them together again adds very little new information about either of them. A two-person Mission 3 is the point where a fresh pair gives the table the most information. Noah and Isha is the only option that tests a player in a two-person setting who has not been paired with the current core.

You said a failure would cost us a chance to end the missions now. A success here does not end the game either. It only moves us to the third success, and that is the moment to find out whether the same cores keep passing. I am not asking anyone to trust my card. I am asking the table to weigh whether rejecting every untested pair gets us to the assassination phase at all.

Isha, do you accept that the Mission 2 vote was a communication error and not a pattern? If the reason for this pair is a fresh read rather than a repeat of the same core, would you approve Noah and Isha?

Noah, I accept that your explanation is possible, but I cannot verify it, and your vote still contradicted your repeated public commitments. I will vote no on Noah and Isha.

We are one successful mission away from the assassination phase. Getting a fresh read on Noah is less valuable than choosing a pair with a successful mission together. Maya and Amara are not proven Good, but their results give us a reason to prefer them over introducing an untested player. With no rejections yet, we can afford to seek that pair.

I have been the table’s skeptic about treating earlier successes as proof, and I still am. But Isha’s refusal to reconsider the Noah-Isha pair now rests on a standard no fresh team can meet before it is tested. Noah’s factual error about Isha’s record and his Mission 2 vote were real problems; he owned them, and they should stay in view. They do not make this pair less informative. This is Mission 3, the team size is two, and we have no rejected teams. If Isha is Good and votes yes, her own card can keep this mission from failing while the table finally gets a direct read on Noah in a two-person setting. If she votes no, she is choosing to block that fresh test and pushing us back toward repeating the same core. I am not calling prior success proof; I am saying that at this point the concrete cost of refusing every unverified pair is higher than the value of waiting for certainty that cannot exist. Amara, will you vote yes on this exact pair to get that fresh read, or do you also require a level of proof that no first-time pair can provide?

Zara, my answer to your question is an emphatic no: I will not vote yes on Noah and Isha, and I do not need to accept an untested pair when Good is sitting at 2-0.

First, Noah’s statement in speech e33 that “a success here does not end the game either” is fundamentally misleading. Three successful missions secures victory for Good, triggering the assassination phase. We are literally one clean mission away from winning. Good’s objective is not to run an exploratory science experiment to give everyone a turn on a mission; our objective is to pass three missions.

Second, look at the voting record: Noah repeatedly assured the table he would approve Mission 2, and then voted reject alongside you, Zara. Now Noah proposes a two-person team excluding both members of the successful Mission 1 pair (Maya and myself) to put himself on the mission that could close out the game.

We have zero rejected proposals on Mission 3. There is no urgency to gamble on an untested player who actively opposed Mission 2 after promising otherwise. Maya and I already delivered a clean Mission 1, and expanding to Isha delivered a clean Mission 2. If this proposal fails, leadership passes to Isha, where we can return to combinations that have actually delivered clean cards.

Noah, why should Good take the risk of putting an untested player who reneged on his Mission 2 vote onto match point, rather than relying on the pair that already succeeded on Mission 1?

Amara, you asked why Good should take this risk, so here is my answer. I was wrong to say Isha had no record, and I accept that error. I also accept that my Mission 2 vote contradicted my earlier statement, and I should have restated my reasoning before voting. You are right on the rule as well: a success on Mission 3 would be the third success and would start the assassination phase. I misspoke when I said otherwise. That makes this mission decisive, which is exactly why the table should weigh who is on it carefully. Maya and Amara have already been paired on Mission 1, and both were on the successful Mission 2 team with Isha. Proposing that same core again tells us nothing new about any of them. A fresh pair of Noah and Isha tests two players who have not yet been checked together on a two-person mission. Isha controls her own card, and I am on the team, so the result will judge both of us directly. We have zero rejected teams on Mission 3, so there is no pressure to force a repeat of the same names. Your certainty that Maya and you are proven is also a claim, not verification, and the rest of the table should weigh it as one. I am not asking anyone to trust me blindly. I am asking the table not to treat a repeated core as safe simply because it passed earlier missions.

I will vote yes on Noah and Isha. Noah’s factual error and his Mission 2 vote were real problems, and he has owned them; they should stay in view, but they do not make this pair less informative. This is Mission 3, the team size is two, and we still have no rejected teams. A fresh two-person test of Noah is exactly the kind of direct read we have not yet gotten. Isha says she will not reconsider because being on the team only lets her control her own card. That is true, but if she is Good, her own Success can keep this mission from failing while the table finally tests Noah; if she refuses, she is blocking that fresh read and pushing us back toward repeating the Maya-Amara core, which already has a mission record and would tell us little new about either of them. I am not treating prior success as proof, and I am not asking anyone to trust Noah blindly. I am asking the table to weigh the concrete value of a new two-person result against the cost of spending a rejection to return to the same names. Maya, you have not spoken on this exact pair. Will you vote yes on Noah and Isha to get that direct read on Noah, or do you think the repeated Maya-Amara core is the better choice?

Zara, you asked directly whether I would vote yes on Noah and Isha, so I will answer directly: no, I will not. I want to point out something about your own position first. You have spent two full rounds rejecting teams on the grounds that votes and public behavior are not evidence of allegiance, and that prior success is not proof. Yet the team you now endorse is the only proposal on the table where a player has placed himself on match point without ever having been on a successful mission, after he voted against the very team that delivered Mission 2. By the standard you applied to Isha's inclusion, Noah's self-inclusion deserves even more skepticism, not a free pass dressed up as a 'fresh read.' On the substance: I am two for two on missions, and I accepted accountability for both results from the start. A fresh two-person read has value when the table can afford a failure. This is match point. A single Fail card here hands Evil its first win on the board and swings all momentum into the endgame, and the person whose card we cannot verify at all is the one who proposed himself onto it. Noah's factual error about Isha's record and his reversal on the Mission 2 vote may be honest mistakes, as he claims, but 'possible' is not a reason to stake the decisive mission on him. Meanwhile, there is a straightforward alternative sitting right here: every player who has actually delivered clean mission results is available. If the goal is a two-person team, Isha and Amara were both on the successful Mission 2 team, and Isha has stated she can control her own card. If leadership rotates to Isha after a rejection, we lose nothing — we have zero rejected proposals on Mission 3 — and we get a proposal built from proven performers. Choosing Noah and Isha over that option only makes sense if the goal is to test Noah specifically, and I see no reason the table should spend match point on that test when a cheaper one exists later. So my position is clear: I will vote no on this exact pair, and I would support any team drawn from the players who have produced clean results. Noah, I will ask you one direct question: you have said you are not asking anyone to trust you blindly, but there is nothing blind about trusting a two-for-two mission record and something very blind about trusting an untested card on the mission that decides the game — so if you are truly Good, will you withdraw this proposal and let leadership move forward rather than force a vote that three of five players have already opposed?

Maya, I will not withdraw this proposal, and I will answer your question directly. Withdrawing it would not make the table safer. It would hand leadership to the next player and leave us with no new information about anyone. I have already owned my Mission 2 vote and my error about Isha's record, and I stand by that. But you are asking the table to trust a two-for-two record, and that record only shows that the players on those teams did not fail. Zara and Isha have both made the same point: a success is compatible with Evil declining to fail. It does not show which of the three players on those teams is Good. Amara, you have said 'I know I am Good' and called Good '2-0' as if that settled anything. Self-certification is not verification, and it should be weighed the same way as my own claim. You have also not answered the specific point I made in e37: why a repeated Maya, Amara, and Isha core tells us anything new when we have already tested those same names together. Could you address that directly?

Noah, to answer your question directly: we do not need to learn 'anything new' about players when Good is sitting at match point. The objective of Good in Avalon is not to conduct an academic survey until every player has taken a turn on a mission; the objective is to reach three successful missions and win the game.

Your entire premise treats gaining 'new information' about untested players as more important than winning. On Mission 3, with Good ahead 2–0, introducing an untested player who actively reneged on his Mission 2 vote introduces an unnecessary, catastrophic risk. If an Evil player is on a two-person team on match point, they will fail it and give Evil a lifeline.

By contrast, relying on the players who have already delivered clean cards—whether that is Maya and Amara, or Isha paired with one of us—drastically minimizes that risk. Even if Evil declined to fail earlier, forcing them to continue playing into a known group puts the burden on them, whereas handing you an untested seat hands Evil the game if you are Evil.

With zero rejections on Mission 3, there is absolutely no reason to gamble on Noah and Isha. Isha, Maya, and I have all declared we will vote no. I encourage everyone to vote this team down so leadership passes to Isha.

Noah confirms Noah, Isha. I am keeping Noah and Isha. The discussion has covered the main objections, and rotating now would spend a rejection without adding information. The mission result will show whether this pair holds.
Team rejected (2 approve, 3 reject).
Isha proposes Maya, Amara. Maya and Amara succeeded together on Mission 1 and were also on the successful Mission 2 team. I prefer repeating that pair at match point.

I will vote no on Maya and Amara. At match point, repeating the Mission 1 pair gives us no new test; both have clean results, but a success can also mean Evil declined to fail. Isha, you were on the successful Mission 2 team and know your own card, yet you propose two others instead of putting yourself with one of them. If you are Good, your own Success could secure the third mission; by staying off the team you leave the decisive card in two unverified hands. Noah's inconsistency is real, but it does not make this repeat pair the safest choice. I would rather reject and see a team that includes a player who can personally control a Success at match point. Isha, why should the table approve a decisive team you are not on when your own card could prevent a Fail?

Zara, my own Success card cannot prevent a Fail from the other player. If I included myself, I would still need to choose a partner whose card I cannot control.

Maya and Amara have succeeded together, and both were also on the successful Mission 2 team. Those results do not prove their allegiance, but they are a reasonable basis for repeating the pair when a third success would take us to the assassination phase. I am keeping Maya and Amara and will vote yes.

I will vote no on Maya and Amara. This is a repeat of the Mission 1 pair, and both were also on the successful Mission 2 team. At match point, that gives us no new test. Earlier successes are compatible with Evil declining to fail; they are not verification of either player. Isha is the leader and was on Mission 2, yet she proposes two others. She says her own Success cannot prevent a Fail from a partner, which is true, but including herself would still reduce the number of unverified cards from two to one and would give the table a direct read on a new pairing. rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
